modules.description: Define the alternative outcome and the experiment you wish you could run.

modules.title: Draw the causal story
modules.description: Distinguish common causes, common effects and causal pathways.

modules.title: Build a fair comparison
modules.description: Standardise, weight and inspect whether the comparison exists.

modules.description: Match a target population and investigate time changes and cutoffs.

lessons.title: One person, two possible outcomes
lessons.short: Calculate an average causal effect when a teaching model reveals both possible outcomes.
lessons.goal: Calculate an average causal effect when a teaching model reveals both possible outcomes.
explain: A causal question asks what would change if we intervened. A treatment is the exposure or action being compared; an outcome is what happens afterward. Here the treatment is attending a specified training course and the outcome is a score one month later.

A potential outcome is the result under a particular treatment choice. Write $Y(1)$ for the score with training and $Y(0)$ for the score without it. A person’s effect is $Y(1)-Y(0)$. The average treatment effect, or ATE, averages these differences over a stated population.

The invented table reveals both potential outcomes for six people. Real data reveal only the outcome under the treatment each person actually received. That missing alternative is the fundamental problem: even a perfectly measured outcome does not reveal an individual causal effect.
lessons.predict: Will the average effect describe every person?
lessons.look: Compare `Individual model effects` with `Population ATE (score points)`. Does the population average tell you whether everyone benefited?
lessons.change: In `with_training`, replace the final `88` with `98`. Run Python again. Which entry in `Individual model effects` changes, and by how much does `Population ATE (score points)` move?
lessons.question: A database records each patient’s treatment and recovery. What is missing for a direct individual effect?
options: The outcome that patient would have had under the other treatment.
Only a larger sample size.
Only the correlation coefficient.
lessons.feedback: An individual effect compares two potential outcomes for the same person. A larger database still observes only one of them per person.
hints: List the two recovery outcomes you would need for the same patient.
Which one can the database record for a person who received treatment?
lessons.limit: The model reveals both outcomes by construction. It does not identify an effect from real observational data.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/

lessons.title: A difference with no treatment effect
lessons.short: Distinguish an observed group difference from a causal effect.
lessons.goal: Distinguish an observed group difference from a causal effect.
explain: An association is a difference or pattern in observed data. A causal effect concerns changing treatment. People who choose a course may already differ from people who do not.

A confounder is a common cause of treatment and outcome. In this model, prior preparation determines both course attendance and score. Training has exactly zero effect: each person’s two potential scores are equal.

We observe mostly well-prepared learners in the trained group. Compute the observed difference, then compare it with the effect revealed by the model. This is the scientific-method question “What else could explain the result?” made numerical.
lessons.predict: Can the observed difference be positive when every causal effect is zero?
lessons.look: Compare `Observed difference` with `Model ATE`. Does the observed contrast recover the effect that the model sets to zero?
lessons.change: Replace the values in the `training` array with `[0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1]`. Run Python again and compare `Observed difference` and `Model ATE`. How does the preparation mix now differ between the trained and untrained groups?
lessons.question: Umbrella users get wetter than nonusers. Which alternative explanation matters?
options: Umbrellas necessarily cause rain.
Rain influences both umbrella use and getting wet.
A strong association rules out alternatives.
lessons.feedback: Rain is a common cause. A comparison must account for the conditions that influenced umbrella use before it can isolate the effect of using one.
hints: Name a condition that could affect both whether someone carries an umbrella and whether they get wet.
Draw arrows from that condition to umbrella use and wetness. Could the two be associated even if the umbrella helps?
lessons.limit: All values are invented; the zero effect is an authored fact, not a conclusion inferred from observed scores.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/

lessons.title: Describe the experiment you wish you had
lessons.short: Specify treatment, eligibility, time zero and follow-up for a causal question.
lessons.goal: Specify treatment, eligibility, time zero and follow-up for a causal question.
explain: A target trial is a description of the randomised experiment that would answer your question. Observational research can try to emulate its protocol even when an actual trial is impossible. Specify eligibility, treatment strategies, assignment, follow-up, outcome and the causal contrast.

Time zero is when eligibility, treatment assignment and follow-up begin together. Classifying people as treated because they eventually take a course can give them guaranteed survival or participation time before treatment. This is often called immortal-time bias.

Consistency means that the observed outcome under the treatment actually received equals the corresponding potential outcome. “Training” needs enough detail to support this claim: a one-hour video and six months of coaching need not represent the same intervention. The code audits two invented protocol descriptions, rather than estimating an effect.
lessons.predict: Which protocol leaves its treatment or start time ambiguous?
lessons.look: Compare the `Vague missing fields` and `Specified missing fields` lines. Which parts of the plan does the program check?
lessons.change: In the protocol named `Vague`, replace `time_zero=None` with `time_zero='eligibility date'`. Run Python again and inspect `Vague missing fields`. Which field remains missing, and what does the check leave unsaid about `any future training`?
lessons.question: A study calls people treated if they attend any time during the next year but counts outcomes from January. What needs repair?
options: Round the outcome more precisely.
Align treatment assignment and the start of follow-up.
Discard all untreated people.
lessons.feedback: Treatment classification using future events can select people who remained eligible long enough to receive treatment. Aligning time zero is part of the design.
hints: Put the start of follow-up and the first opportunity to receive treatment on a timeline.
Before taking the course, what must someone do to remain eligible long enough to join the treated group?
lessons.limit: This is a protocol checklist, not a causal estimator. It cannot automatically verify consistency, eligibility or absence of interference.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/

lessons.title: Draw the alternative explanation
lessons.short: Identify the adjustment variable for a simple common-cause diagram.
lessons.goal: Identify the adjustment variable for a simple common-cause diagram.
explain: A directed acyclic graph, or DAG, represents causal assumptions with arrows and no directed loops. An arrow means a proposed direct causal influence at the chosen level of detail. It is a claim to justify using subject knowledge, not a fact discovered from correlation alone.

Let $L$ be preparation, $A$ training and $Y$ score. The diagram has $L \to A$, $L \to Y$ and $A \to Y$. The route $A \leftarrow L \to Y$ is a backdoor path: it links treatment and outcome through a common cause.

Adjustment compares outcomes within levels of a suitable measured common cause, then combines these comparisons for a target population. In this simple graph, conditioning on preparation blocks the backdoor path. The invented table makes that within-group comparison visible.
lessons.predict: Will the within-preparation contrasts agree with the overall contrast?
lessons.look: Compare `Overall difference` and `Within-preparation differences`. Which uses people from the same preparation group for both treatment choices?
lessons.change: Replace `counts` with `np.array([[50, 50], [50, 50]])`. Run Python again and compare `Overall difference`, `Within-preparation differences` and `Equal-population standardised difference`. Why do the overall and adjusted comparisons now agree?
lessons.question: In a diagram, age causes treatment choice and outcome. Neither is a cause of age. What is age’s role?
options: Mediator.
Common cause to consider for adjustment.
Outcome of treatment.
lessons.feedback: Age lies on a backdoor path through a common cause. Under this simple graph, adjusting for it blocks that path; real graphs may require other variables too.
hints: Draw the two arrows from age to the variables named in the question.
Trace the path from treatment back through age to outcome. What happens if you compare people of the same age?
lessons.limit: The diagram assumes preparation is measured adequately and captures all common causes. Observed balance on one variable cannot establish that assumption.
source: Pearl · Causal diagrams for empirical research
https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/82.4.669

lessons.title: When adjustment creates a problem
lessons.short: Show how conditioning on a common effect creates an association.
lessons.goal: Show how conditioning on a common effect creates an association.
explain: A collider is a common effect of two variables: $A \to S \leftarrow U$. Without conditioning on $S$ or its descendants, this path is blocked. Selecting or adjusting for $S$ can open the path.

Imagine independent skill and luck, each a fair coin. Admission happens if either is high. Among admitted people, someone with low skill must have high luck; someone with high skill may have either. Selection creates dependence even though the two causes began independently.

The code enumerates the entire four-person teaching population, so no sampling uncertainty obscures the mechanism. In observational studies, selection into a hospital, employment or a survey can create similar structures. The direction of arrows determines whether adjustment helps.
lessons.predict: Among admitted people, will skill and luck still be independent?
lessons.look: Compare `Population correlation` with `Correlation after selecting admission`. Does selecting on admission change the relationship between skill and luck?
lessons.change: Change `admitted = (skill + luck) >= 1` to `admitted = (skill + luck) <= 1`. Before you select Run Python again, list the three admitted skill-and-luck pairs. Compare `Correlation after selecting admission` for the two rules. Does the sign tell you which rule was used?
lessons.question: Treatment and underlying illness both cause a follow-up test to be ordered. Should you automatically restrict to tested patients?
options: Yes, selection always improves comparability.
Yes, because the test happens later.
No; testing may be a collider and induce selection bias.
lessons.feedback: Testing is a common effect in the stated diagram. Conditioning on it can connect treatment to illness; a valid design needs a justification for the selected population.
hints: Draw separate arrows from treatment and illness to the decision to order a test.
Among tested patients, what might learning that a person was untreated imply about how they came to be tested?
lessons.limit: This deterministic population illustrates selection. It does not imply every selected dataset has a negative association or that every post-treatment variable is a collider.
source: Pearl · Causal diagrams for empirical research
https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/82.4.669

lessons.title: Which effect are you asking for?
lessons.short: Distinguish a total effect from a direct pathway in a causal model.
lessons.goal: Distinguish a total effect from a direct pathway in a causal model.
explain: A mediator lies on a causal pathway from treatment to outcome. Training may increase practice, which increases score. For the total effect, both the direct training pathway and the pathway through practice count.

Our authored linear model says practice equals twice training and score equals three times training plus four times practice. Increasing training by one therefore changes score by $3+4\times2=11$. Holding practice fixed would leave only the direct coefficient of three.

Adjusting for a mediator can remove part of the effect you wanted. Estimating direct effects from observational data requires additional assumptions, including control of mediator–outcome confounding. Reading a coefficient from this known structural model is easier than identifying it in real data.
lessons.predict: Will holding practice fixed retain the whole training effect?
lessons.look: Compare `Total model effect` with `Effect with practice held at zero`. Which includes the training-to-practice pathway?
lessons.change: Change `training_to_practice` from `2` to `0`. Run Python again and compare `Total model effect` and `Effect with practice held at zero`. Why do the two contrasts now agree?
lessons.question: A policy increases income, which improves housing, which improves health. For the total policy effect, housing is…
options: A mediator whose pathway contributes to the effect.
Always a baseline confounder.
Evidence that the policy has no effect.
lessons.feedback: Housing transmits part of the policy effect in the stated model. Blocking this pathway changes the causal question.
hints: Trace the arrows from policy through income and housing to health.
If you fixed housing at the same value for everyone, which part of the policy effect would be left out?
lessons.limit: The structural coefficients are authored. No regression on real observational data has identified these direct or indirect effects.
source: Pearl · Causal diagrams for empirical research
https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/82.4.669

lessons.title: Compare the same population twice
lessons.short: Calculate an adjusted average effect by standardisation.
lessons.goal: Calculate an adjusted average effect by standardisation.
explain: Standardisation predicts each treatment’s average outcome in the same target population. For each baseline group, calculate its treated and untreated outcome means, then weight both sets by the target group proportions.

Identification means the causal quantity can be expressed using observed-data quantities under stated assumptions. Here we need conditional exchangeability (no unmeasured common causes within baseline groups), positivity (both treatments possible in each target group), and consistency. For this simple individual treatment interpretation, assume no interference between people.

The low-preparation group has a two-point contrast and the high-preparation group a ten-point contrast. Equal weighting and a target with 80% low preparation answer different population questions. Neither target is automatically the correct one.
lessons.predict: Will changing the target mix change the average effect?
lessons.look: Find `Target means without/with`. Both means use the same target mix. How does `Target average difference` compare with `Equal-mix difference`?
lessons.change: Change the `target` proportions from `[0.8, 0.2]` to `[0.2, 0.8]`. This puts 80% of the target population in the high-preparation group. Run Python again. Which of `Target average difference` and `Equal-mix difference` changes, and why?
lessons.question: Two populations have the same group-specific effects but different group proportions. Must their ATEs match?
options: Yes, an effect is always universal.
No, average effects can differ with the population mix.
Only if both studies have small p-values.
lessons.feedback: A population average weights its members’ effects. Different mixes can produce different averages even when group-specific effects agree.
hints: Try two groups whose treatment effects are 2 and 10 points in both populations.
Compute an average with half the people in each group. What happens if almost everyone is in the group with the 10-point effect?
lessons.limit: The group means are invented and treated as known. Standardisation does not repair unmeasured confounding or unsupported treatment groups.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/

lessons.title: Give underrepresented choices more weight
lessons.short: Calculate inverse-probability weights for a known treatment mechanism.
lessons.goal: Calculate inverse-probability weights for a known treatment mechanism.
explain: A propensity score is the probability of receiving treatment given baseline variables. It describes treatment assignment, not the probability that a person benefits. Inverse-probability weighting gives more influence to people whose observed treatment was less likely.

For treated people the weight is $1/e(L)$, where $e(L)$ is the propensity score. For untreated people it is $1/(1-e(L))$. We use normalised weighted means, also called Hájek means, and subtract the untreated mean from the treated mean.

This constructed population has 20% treated in one baseline group and 80% in another. The true propensities are supplied. With consistency, positivity, conditional exchangeability and no interference, weighting can target the population ATE. Estimated propensities introduce additional modelling and uncertainty.
lessons.predict: Which treated people receive weight five?
lessons.look: Compare `Observed difference` with `Weighted difference`. Find the largest values in `Weights` and check which people received the less likely treatment for their group.
lessons.change: Change `treatment_effect` from `5` to `-3`. Run Python again and compare the signs of `Observed difference` and `Weighted difference`. Which recovers the sign of the effect set in the model?
lessons.question: What does a propensity score of 0.1 mean?
options: A 10% probability of benefit.
A 10% outcome risk.
A 10% treatment probability given the baseline information.
lessons.feedback: The propensity score models treatment assignment. It does not directly measure outcome risk or treatment benefit.
hints: Decide what event the probability refers to before interpreting 0.1.
For people with the same baseline information, does the score describe who receives treatment or what happens afterward?
lessons.limit: Exact recovery is constructed here. Correct weighting in observed data still depends on measured confounders, assignment modelling and overlap.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/

lessons.title: When the comparison is missing
lessons.short: Diagnose an unsupported treatment comparison before estimating an effect.
lessons.goal: Diagnose an unsupported treatment comparison before estimating an effect.
explain: Positivity requires a nonzero chance of each treatment within every baseline group needed for the target effect. If everyone above a threshold receives treatment, the data contain no untreated comparison above that threshold.

Near violations produce very large inverse-probability weights. Effective sample size, calculated here as $(\sum w)^2/\sum w^2$, is a descriptive measure of weight concentration. It is not a complete standard-error calculation.

Trimming extreme weights can trade variance for bias and may change the estimand, the precise quantity being estimated. Restricting the target population to overlap can be sensible, but the population change must be reported. A statistical model can extrapolate into an empty cell without supplying new evidence.
lessons.predict: Will one huge weight make ten observations behave like ten equally weighted observations?
lessons.look: Compare `Records` with `Weight-based effective sample size`. The separate counts table produces `Groups with an empty treatment cell`. Which diagnostic describes concentrated weights, and which describes a missing comparison?
lessons.change: In `weights`, replace the final `100.` with `1.` while leaving `counts` as prepared. Run Python again and compare `Weight-based effective sample size` and `Groups with an empty treatment cell`. Which changes?
lessons.question: Every severely ill patient receives treatment. Can these data alone identify an untreated mean for severely ill patients without extrapolation?
options: No; that treatment comparison lacks support.
Yes; add more decimal places.
Yes; weights create untreated outcomes.
lessons.feedback: There are no untreated severe patients in this design. Weighting cannot manufacture their outcomes; a model-based extrapolation requires additional assumptions.
hints: Make a row for severely ill patients with a treated column and an untreated column.
Can a weighted average use untreated outcomes from a cell with no people in it?
lessons.limit: Weight-based effective sample size is a diagnostic. These invented counts do not evaluate balance on unmeasured variables.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/

lessons.title: Match people, then name the target
lessons.short: Calculate an effect among treated people using exact baseline matches.
lessons.goal: Calculate an effect among treated people using exact baseline matches.
explain: Matching selects untreated comparisons with similar baseline variables to treated people. Here we use exact matching on a binary preparation group. For each treated person, the untreated group mean supplies the comparison.

This targets the average treatment effect among the treated, or ATT, when consistency, conditional exchangeability and untreated comparison support hold for the treated population. ATT and ATE need not match when treatment effects vary and the treated population differs from the whole population.

Exact matching on one recorded variable does not guarantee comparability on everything else. In real work, inspect baseline balance, discarded observations, replacement rules and the target population. Do not match on consequences of treatment just because they predict outcomes well.
lessons.predict: Will the treated-population effect equal the equal-mix population effect?
lessons.look: Compare `ATT`, the average effect among the treated, with `ATE in an equal-mix population`. Which group proportions does each average use?
lessons.change: In the editor, set `treated_group` to `np.array([0, 0, 0, 1])` and `treated_score` to `np.array([42., 42., 42., 80.])`. Run Python again. Which of `ATT` and `ATE in an equal-mix population` changes when the treated group has more people with low preparation?
lessons.question: A matching analysis drops treated patients with no comparable controls. Its effect applies directly to…
options: Every eligible patient automatically.
The retained treated population, under the matching assumptions.
Only the discarded patients.
lessons.feedback: Dropping unsupported treated people changes the target. Report who remains and avoid automatically generalising their estimate to all treated people.
hints: Identify which treated patients still contribute a comparison after matching.
Would the resulting average describe patients whose outcomes were left out of that average?
lessons.limit: Control means are invented and known without estimation error. Real matching adds uncertainty, support decisions and unmeasured-confounding concerns.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/

lessons.title: Subtract the change that would happen anyway
lessons.short: Compute a difference-in-differences estimate and expose its key assumption.
lessons.goal: Compute a difference-in-differences estimate and expose its key assumption.
explain: Difference-in-differences compares the before-to-after change in an exposed group with the change in a comparison group. Subtracting the comparison change can remove a shared time trend.

The parallel-trends assumption says that, without treatment, the two groups’ mean outcomes would have changed by the same amount over the relevant period. It concerns unobserved untreated outcomes after treatment; matching pre-treatment trends can support its plausibility but cannot prove it.

Our two-period model includes a shared six-point time change and a four-point policy effect. Add an unobserved group-specific trend to see the estimate mix that trend with the effect. Also needed are no anticipation, no policy spillovers to the comparison group and a comparable population over time.
lessons.predict: What happens if the treated group would improve three extra points even without the policy?
lessons.look: Compare `Difference-in-differences` with `Authored effect`. What change does the comparison group supply in the prepared example?
lessons.change: Change `group_specific_trend` from `0` to `3`. Run Python again and compare `Difference-in-differences` with `Authored effect`. How far does the estimate move, and which assumption does that extra trend violate?
lessons.question: Two regions had similar pre-policy trends. Does that establish parallel untreated trends after the policy?
options: Yes, with certainty.
Only if the p-value is small.
No; it provides context but the post-policy counterfactual remains unobserved.
lessons.feedback: Pre-period evidence can challenge or support a design. It cannot reveal the treated group’s unobserved post-policy trajectory without treatment.
hints: Name the trajectory the design needs for the policy group after the policy starts.
Can the trends before the policy reveal what would have happened later to that group without it?
lessons.limit: This is the simple two-group, two-period design. Staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects require additional methods.
source: World Bank · Impact Evaluation in Practice
https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/sief-trust-fund/publication/impact-evaluation-in-practice

lessons.title: Look just beside the cutoff
lessons.short: Distinguish a local cutoff effect from a population-wide effect.
lessons.goal: Distinguish a local cutoff effect from a population-wide effect.
explain: Regression discontinuity uses a treatment assignment cutoff. In a sharp design, everyone above the cutoff is treated and everyone below is untreated. Compare outcomes just on either side, where baseline characteristics may be similar.

The continuity assumption says untreated and treated potential-outcome means would change smoothly through the cutoff in the absence of the treatment switch. Precise manipulation of the assignment score, another policy at the same cutoff, or a discontinuous population change threatens the comparison.

The code subtracts local means under a known linear trend. A finite window includes some baseline-score difference, so its contrast is only an approximation to the discontinuity. A smaller window reduces this trend contamination here; real samples then lose precision.
lessons.predict: Will a wider window mix more of the smooth baseline trend into a raw contrast?
lessons.look: Compare `Raw local difference` across the three `Window` values with `True discontinuity at cutoff`. What changes as the window narrows?
lessons.change: In `y = 50 + 0.8 * score + effect * a`, change the coefficient of `score` from `0.8` to `0`. Run Python again and compare `Raw local difference` across the three windows. Why do the raw differences now agree?
lessons.question: A scholarship cutoff effect is credible near a score of 80. Does it directly identify the effect for score 20?
options: Yes, all treated effects must be equal.
No; generalising far from the cutoff needs further assumptions.
Yes, if the window is narrow enough.
lessons.feedback: Regression discontinuity identifies a local effect under its assumptions. A narrow window improves local comparability, not population-wide transportability.
hints: Where on the score scale does the design get the comparisons it uses?
What assumption would let a comparison near 80 tell you about a person with score 20?
lessons.limit: Noise-free invented data illustrate locality. A real analysis needs appropriate local regression, bandwidth choices, uncertainty and design diagnostics.
source: World Bank · Impact Evaluation in Practice
https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/sief-trust-fund/publication/impact-evaluation-in-practice

lessons.title: An encouragement is not the treatment
lessons.short: Interpret a simple instrumental-variable estimate for people whose treatment changes.
lessons.goal: Interpret a simple instrumental-variable estimate for people whose treatment changes.
explain: An instrument is a variable that shifts treatment and can identify a causal effect under special assumptions. Consider a random course invitation. Some people always attend, some never attend, and some attend only when invited. Those last people are compliers.

For a binary instrument, the Wald ratio divides the invitation–outcome difference by the invitation–attendance difference. Under independence, relevance, exclusion (invitation affects the outcome only through attendance), monotonicity (no one attends only when not invited), consistency and no interference, it identifies a local average treatment effect for compliers.

The code uses an enumerated population with equal type proportions in both invitation groups. A direct motivational effect of invitation violates exclusion. The ratio then combines attendance and invitation effects; a weak effect on attendance can amplify that problem.
lessons.predict: Will a direct invitation effect be divided by the attendance change too?
lessons.look: Compare `Wald ratio` with `attendance_effect` in the prepared code. Find which printed quantities form the numerator and denominator.
lessons.change: Change `direct_invitation_effect` from `0` to `1`. Run Python again and compare `Attendance change`, `Invitation outcome change` and `Wald ratio` with your first run. Which change explains why the ratio moves away from the unchanged attendance effect?
lessons.question: A valid random invitation identifies an attendance effect through the Wald ratio. Whose effect is it?
options: All people automatically.
People who would always attend.
Compliers whose attendance changes because of invitation.
lessons.feedback: With the stated assumptions, the local average effect concerns compliers. Extending it to everyone requires assumptions about effect variation.
hints: List people who always attend, never attend, or attend only when invited.
Whose attendance can explain the difference in attendance between the invitation groups?
lessons.limit: The exclusion restriction cannot generally be verified from the observed instrument, treatment and outcome alone. This example supplies it by construction.
source: Angrist, Imbens & Rubin · Identification of causal effects using instrumental variables

lessons.title: A precise answer to the wrong question
lessons.short: Separate sampling uncertainty from confounding bias.
lessons.goal: Separate sampling uncertainty from confounding bias.
explain: A confidence interval quantifies sampling uncertainty under a specified procedure and assumptions. It does not automatically include systematic error from confounding, measurement or selection.

This simulation makes treatment more common among people with high baseline scores. Treatment adds exactly two points, but the unadjusted group contrast includes the baseline difference. Larger samples make the wrong contrast more precise.

We use the bootstrap: resample whole independent people with replacement and recalculate the unadjusted difference. The percentile interval is an approximate interval for that observed-data contrast. It cannot turn the contrast into an identified causal effect.
lessons.predict: Will a narrow interval necessarily contain the authored causal effect?
lessons.look: Compare `Approximate 95% bootstrap interval` with `Authored causal effect`. Does the interval for the unadjusted contrast contain the effect that generated the data?
lessons.change: Change `n` from `2000` to `8000`. Run Python again. Compare the width of `Approximate 95% bootstrap interval` with your first run. Separately compare the distance from `Unadjusted contrast` to `Authored causal effect`. Does the narrower interval fix the bias?
lessons.question: An unadjusted estimate is precise but treatment depends on prior health. What has precision established?
options: That confounding is absent.
That the statistical procedure estimates the observed contrast precisely under its assumptions.
That randomisation occurred.
lessons.feedback: Precision concerns variability. Identification requires a credible link from the observed comparison to the causal question.
hints: Ask what would vary if you repeatedly sampled people using the same design.
If prior health still differs between treatment groups, does measuring the observed difference more precisely change what it compares?
lessons.limit: People are independent in the simulation. The bootstrap procedure is approximate; clustered or dependent data need a suitable resampling unit.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/

lessons.title: How strong would the missing cause need to be?
lessons.short: Calculate a simple sensitivity analysis for an unmeasured binary common cause.
lessons.goal: Calculate a simple sensitivity analysis for an unmeasured binary common cause.
explain: A sensitivity analysis asks how conclusions change under explicit departures from an assumption. It does not discover whether a missing confounder exists. It makes the size of a proposed alternative explanation inspectable.

Suppose an unmeasured binary variable adds a constant amount to the outcome and has different prevalence in treated and untreated groups. In an additive model without interactions, its contribution to the observed contrast is its outcome effect times the prevalence difference.

Subtract that hypothetical bias from a four-point observed contrast. This is an algebraic scenario analysis, not a fully adjusted estimate. Plausible parameter ranges need subject knowledge or external evidence; choosing convenient values after seeing the result is not validation.
lessons.predict: Which combination could explain the whole four-point contrast?
lessons.look: In the output, compare `Hypothetical U effect`, the proposed effect of the missing cause, with `Remaining contrast`. Which proposed effect leaves zero contrast under the prepared prevalence gap?
lessons.change: Change `prevalence_gap` from `0.4` to `0.2`. Run Python again and inspect `Bias` and `Remaining contrast` for the same proposed effects. Use the pattern to work out which effect would leave zero contrast under the new gap.
lessons.question: A sensitivity analysis finds a confounder could explain an effect. What follows?
options: Such a confounder definitely exists.
The effect is definitely zero.
The conclusion depends on whether that confounding scenario is plausible.
lessons.feedback: Sensitivity analysis evaluates hypothetical departures. It neither proves a missing cause exists nor proves the original assumptions hold.
hints: Separate what the analysis assumes about a missing cause from what it observes.
If the model says what a given missing cause could explain, what evidence would make that cause and its strength plausible?
lessons.limit: The bias formula assumes an additive, constant outcome contribution and a suitable prevalence contrast. It omits sampling uncertainty and more complex confounding structures.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/

lessons.title: Who is left in the analysis?
lessons.short: Demonstrate how differential outcome observation changes a treatment contrast.
lessons.goal: Demonstrate how differential outcome observation changes a treatment contrast.
explain: An outcome can be missing because people drop out, do not answer or are not measured. A complete-case analysis compares only observed outcomes. If observation depends on treatment and outcome-related factors, it can select different kinds of people in each group.

In this finite model everyone gains exactly five points under treatment. But low-scoring treated people are missing while every untreated outcome is observed. Comparing available cases adds selection to the treatment effect.

Inverse observation weighting or multiple imputation may help under appropriate missingness and model assumptions, but neither is automatic. Report how many outcomes are missing, why observation differs, and what assumptions would recover the target population. The toy model reveals missing scores only so you can audit the mechanism.
lessons.predict: Will the complete-case contrast still be five?
lessons.look: Compare `Full model effect` with `Available-case contrast`. `Observed fractions` lists untreated and treated observation rates in that order. Which group lost outcomes in the example?
lessons.change: Replace the values in `observed1` with `[True, True, True, True]`. Run Python again. Compare `Available-case contrast` and `Observed fractions` with your first run. Which treated scores returned to the calculation?
lessons.question: Half the treated outcomes and none of the control outcomes are missing. Is discarding the missing rows guaranteed unbiased?
options: No; the observation mechanism and target population matter.
Yes; software ignores blank cells correctly.
Yes; equal treatment effects guarantee it.
lessons.feedback: A complete-case analysis targets selected observations unless assumptions connect them to the target population. The missingness mechanism matters.
hints: Identify who supplies the available treated outcomes and who supplies the available control outcomes.
Could the average of the missing treated scores differ from the average of the treated scores you still observe?
lessons.limit: Both potential outcomes are revealed only in the invented model. In real data the missing scores are unknown, and their distribution cannot generally be verified from observed rows alone.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/

lessons.title: Will the effect travel?
lessons.short: Recalculate an effect for a new population and recognise a spillover limit.
lessons.goal: Recalculate an effect for a new population and recognise a spillover limit.
explain: An effect estimated in one setting may not apply to another. Effect modification means a treatment effect differs by a baseline characteristic. Transporting an estimate requires considering the new population mix and whether the relevant response relationships remain applicable.

We already standardised within a study. Here the same arithmetic transports group-specific effects to a destination population. This requires the supplied group effects to apply there, sufficient overlap in those groups, and adequate measurement of characteristics that explain effect differences.

Population reweighting does not fix interference: one person’s treatment may affect another person’s outcome. For example, training can spread knowledge to untreated coworkers. A study of individual offers at one uptake level may not estimate the effect of training an entire workplace.
lessons.predict: If experienced learners benefit less, which population has the smaller average effect?
lessons.look: Compare `Study average effect` with `Destination average under transport assumptions`. Which average gives more weight to the group with the smaller effect?
lessons.change: Change `destination_mix` from `[0.2, 0.8]` to `[0.5, 0.5]`. Run Python again and compare the two averages with your first run. Then name a change in how people interact that changing group weights would miss.
lessons.question: Training improves untreated coworkers’ scores through shared knowledge. Which usual individual-treatment assumption is threatened?
options: Equal sample sizes.
No interference between people.
Arithmetic averaging.
lessons.feedback: Coworkers’ outcomes depend on others’ training assignments. A treatment strategy and analysis that account for spillovers may be needed.
hints: Identify a worker whose score changes despite receiving no training.
Which assumption lets you describe a person's outcome using only their own training assignment?
lessons.limit: Transportability and no interference are assumptions here. Reweighting does not establish them or cover unrepresented populations.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/

lessons.title: Make the reasoning inspectable
lessons.short: Write a causal conclusion that separates the estimate, identification assumptions and limits.
lessons.goal: Write a causal conclusion that separates the estimate, identification assumptions and limits.
explain: A reproducible calculation is necessary but does not by itself establish a causal claim. Someone should be able to inspect the question, target population, treatment timing, causal diagram, comparison strategy, data provenance, estimate and uncertainty.

This final example compares an unadjusted contrast with a standardised contrast in an invented two-group population. Before calling the adjusted number causal, name consistency, conditional exchangeability, positivity and no interference, and explain why the chosen baseline variable is appropriate.

Use the report below to describe your target trial, assumptions, result and a next test that could challenge the conclusion. You can export it with the exact last completed execution. The example has known cell means; it deliberately supplies no confidence interval or real-world finding. A real study needs a design-appropriate uncertainty analysis and provenance for its observations.
lessons.predict: What does the arithmetic show, and what must the design justify?
lessons.look: Compare `Unadjusted contrast (points)` with `Standardised contrast (points)`. Which uses the same preparation proportions for both treatment strategies?
lessons.change: In the second row of `means`, replace the treated mean `75.` with `80.`. Run Python again and compare `Unadjusted contrast (points)` and `Standardised contrast (points)`. Do the two preparation groups still have the same effect? Explain why the target proportions now affect the standardised contrast.
lessons.question: Which conclusion is defensible after an observational adjustment?
options: The model proves there are no unmeasured causes.
The adjusted estimate is causal because it is reproducible.
Under the stated identification and modelling assumptions, the adjusted contrast estimates the named target effect.
lessons.feedback: A causal interpretation links a specific estimand to a justified design and assumptions. Reproducibility checks the calculation; it does not verify every assumption.
hints: Write down the target effect using a population, treatment choices and outcome.
What connects the adjustment you computed with the counterfactual comparison in that target effect?
lessons.limit: This capstone uses invented aggregate cell means with no sampling-error model. It is a reasoning and reporting exercise, not evidence that training improves real scores.
source: Hernán & Robins · Causal Inference: What If
https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/
